a35.speaker: Verna Sinimbo, Kavango West Governor
a35.speech: Visited members of the family affected by a suspected food poisoning incident at Rundu hospital, pledging her full support. ; Assured the family that the government would provide assistance where needed.

a128.speaker: Government ministers (Benin)
a128.speech: Made declarations regretting the National Assembly’s rejection of the examination of the constitutional revision bill.

a128.speaker: Parfaite de Banamè, young woman leader of the Banamè church
a128.speech: In an audio file, defends the constitutional revision bill while criticising all those who campaigned against the project: “Talon, for whom people cried ‘hosanna! hosanna!’, today we have reached ‘crucify him! crucify him! Money is not circulating!’ It is easy money that is not circulating. The Beninese want one thing and its opposite! Look at Rosine Soglo, an elderly lady who should be playing with her grandsons and instead finds herself in the Assembly making a racket, an old woman who disturbs the country without hiding it (…) Since parliament rejected the revision bill, do we already have money in the country? Young people should ask themselves questions! The politicians are manipulating the country (…) The economic crisis is universal, it is not only in Benin! Banamè supports and will always support Talon. We, we take responsibility for our choice… It is not because one is hungry that one must start barking everywhere. At Banamè, we support the truth and the well-being of this people.”

a299.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State
a299.speech: Issued a notification signalling that the Trump administration would fold USAID's independent functions into the Department of State under executive control.

a299.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State
a299.speech: Announced on social media that 83 percent of USAID's contracts have been cancelled.

a299.speaker: Tammy Bruce, State Department spokesperson
a299.speech: Said department officials "have notified Congress on their intent to undertake a reorganisation that would involve realigning certain USAID functions to the department by July 1, 2025, and discontinuing the remaining USAID functions that do not align with administrative priorities".

a299.speaker: Tammy Bruce, State Department spokesperson
a299.speech: Denied that the dismantling of USAID would affect the country's ability to respond to international disasters like Friday's earthquakes in Myanmar and Thailand: "We are ready to move now. So there has been no impact on our ability to perform those duties, those requests for aid if and when they come in."

a299.speaker: Tammy Bruce, State Department spokesperson
a299.speech: On the layoffs: "With any major change, there's going to be disruption," adding that the layoffs were not unexpected ; "We've been waiting for this conclusion. It has arrived. I can't speak to the number of people who will not be a foreign service officer at this point. I can't say if it's going to be every single one." ; "It's a restructuring essentially... Like any restructuring, there will inevitably be disruptions from Secretary Rubio down. We are committed to ensuring that USAID personnel remain safe and that the agency's ongoing lifesaving aid programmes remain both intact and operational." ; tied the layoffs to the Trump administration's campaign to eliminate alleged "waste and fraud and abuse".

a299.speaker: Internal memorandum to USAID employees (obtained by US media)
a299.speech: Warned that all positions -- save those required by law -- would be eliminated.

a299.speaker: Judge Theodore Chuang, US federal judge
a299.speech: Ruled that Musk and his Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) "likely violated the United States Constitution in multiple ways" by dismantling USAID, and wrote that Musk and DOGE "deprived the public's elected representatives in Congress of their constitutional authority to decide whether, when and how to close down an agency created by Congress"; through a temporary injunction ordered DOGE and Musk to stop their efforts to slash USAID's staff and contracts.

a299.speaker: Elon Musk, adviser and head of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE)
a299.speech: Has previously boasted that he was involved in "feeding USAID into the wood chipper."

a304.speaker: Nigerien authorities / government
a304.speech: Accused the EU of having "unilaterally" redistributed 1.3 million euros of EU humanitarian aid to foreign NGOs operating in Niger without their having been informed beforehand; said they were carrying out an audit and called on the EU to do the same; said Niger had requested the replacement of the EU ambassador before his recall.

a304.speaker: Nigerien Ministry of Foreign Affairs (statement)
a304.speech: Said it had summoned Mr Da Franca on 14 October to "put an end to the operations" of delivering the aid, before "noting" that they continued; said the government concluded that "collaboration" with Salvador Pinto da Franca was "no longer possible" and officially requested "his recall and replacement as soon as possible"; stated that Niger "has never issued an appeal for international humanitarian aid following the floods" ; "The announcement of this unsolicited aid appeared on social media two weeks before the Nigerien authorities were officially informed, which is contrary to diplomatic practice."

a304.speaker: European Union
a304.speech: Expressed its "profound disagreement" after the challenge to the aid management arrangements and announced the recall of its ambassador to Niger, Salvador Pinto da Franca, for "consultations" in Brussels; stated that it "wishes to continue supporting the population."

a607.speaker: Standard Bank Plc
a607.speech: Has welcomed the new administration's commitment to restoring economic stability, predictability, and strong governance, describing the move as a critical step toward rebuilding investor confidence and national growth.

a607.speaker: Phillip Madinga, Standard Bank Chief Executive Officer
a607.speech: Said the bank is ready to work hand in hand with government and other key stakeholders to help implement President Arthur Peter Mutharika's plan to tackle the country's pressing macroeconomic challenges: "Attracting foreign direct investment from key economies such as the United States and China, as outlined in President Mutharika's inauguration speech, is crucial to unlocking Malawi's growth potential and achieving meaningful recovery."

a607.speaker: Phillip Madinga, Standard Bank Chief Executive Officer
a607.speech: Commended the President's determination to renew diplomatic relations with the United States, saying his special friendship with U.S. President Donald Trump could pave the way for stronger economic and trade ties: "Easing diplomatic hurdles with the U.S. should set the stage for dialogue aimed at finding lasting solutions for Malawi's economy, trade, and diplomatic relations."

a607.speaker: Phillip Madinga, Standard Bank Chief Executive Officer
a607.speech: Noted that the loss of development and technical assistance following USAID's departure had negatively affected the country, emphasizing the need for renewed engagement and open dialogue to explore sustainable solutions.

a607.speaker: Phillip Madinga, Standard Bank Chief Executive Officer
a607.speech: Highlighted the importance of a strong public-private partnership during the next three months of the government's transition period, describing it as a crucial window to re-set the country's economic trajectory ; "Malawi must now reaffirm its resolve to restore stability through fiscal discipline, good governance, and meaningful dialogue with bilateral and multilateral donors and creditors. The foundation for a stronger, more resilient economy must be laid now."

a642.speaker: Donald MacKay, trade expert and head of XA Global Trade Advisors
a642.speech: “Agoa has essentially ended tonight” ; said the new 30% duty on SA, coming on top of the 25% smacked on auto imports from all countries on 26 March, had effectively negated SA’s lucrative duty-free exports into the US under the African Growth and Opportunity Act (Agoa) ; “Agoa, to my mind, has essentially ended tonight … with a 30% tariff, the 3.5% benefit on average that we get out of Agoa has truly become meaningless.”

a642.speaker: Donald MacKay, trade expert and head of XA Global Trade Advisors
a642.speech: noted in a video message to his clients that the Trump administration had imposed the 30% tariff on SA imports based on a formula of halving what it said was the average tariff of 60% for US imports into SA, but said SA’s tariffs on US imports averaged only 7.5%: “If we follow President Trump’s logic, what we should be facing is something like a 3.75% tariff instead. Of course, facts don’t matter that much here.” ; said that last year, SA exported about R153-billion worth of products to the US, half of which were minerals.

a642.speaker: Donald MacKay, trade expert and head of XA Global Trade Advisors
a642.speech: said BMW and Mercedes-Benz, which export significant numbers of vehicles to the US, would be among the hardest hit by the tariff ; added that it was not clear if the 30% tariff would be added to the 25% auto tariff hike ; said it was not clear how the US would replace the SA cars: “It’s very easy to sign off on a tariff policy, much harder to build a factory. The US is not miraculously going to have the capacity to build all of these cars, so car prices will certainly rise.” ; noted that the new import tariffs had not been applied evenly, with Brazil, which competes with SA vehicles in the US market, receiving only a 10% tariff increase.

a642.speaker: Official sources
a642.speech: Said 35-40% of SA’s 2024 exports would be exempt from the 30% tariff, mostly minerals and energy ; told Daily Maverick that the 30% tariff would not be added to the 25% auto tariff.

a642.speaker: Jee-A van der Linde, senior economist at Oxford Economics Africa
a642.speech: “I think many underestimated this” ; “People were blindsided in the same way they were with USAID removal. The Trump administration moves fast and it slices deep.”

a642.speaker: Jee-A van der Linde, senior economist at Oxford Economics Africa
a642.speech: “This is not really about economics. This is about sending a message. Even an economics 101 student would look at this and say: ‘What is this?’ There’s no coefficient for the relationship between countries. That should be the first red flag.” ; “This isn’t economics. It’s politics masquerading as policy.” ; calls it “a non-equilibrium world” — a reality where unpredictability is the new norm.

a642.speaker: Jee-A van der Linde, senior economist at Oxford Economics Africa
a642.speech: “Companies don’t really have time to adjust. Smaller players will be hit first.”

a642.speaker: Kush Desai, White House spokesperson
a642.speech: quoted the US Trade Representative formula that attempts to mechanically adjust tariff rates until trade balances equalise — US exports to a country minus US imports from that country, divided by US imports from that country.

a642.speaker: Izak Odendaal, wealth strategist at Old Mutual Investment Group
a642.speech: echoed the critique in an interview with Daily Maverick: “It’s just a bit crazy. There’s no real link to economic theory or actual trade dynamics. If you’re serious about trade fairness, you don’t go after Lesotho with a 50% tariff.” ; “It’s 1950s industrial policy thinking in a world of global supply chains. Trade today is about intermediate goods. You can end up hurting your own exporters just as much as foreign ones.” ; “The idea that he would be a dealmaker has gone out the window. There doesn’t seem to be a clear negotiation process here.”

a642.speaker: Economists (unnamed)
a642.speech: highlighted inconsistencies that raise further red flags, among them the inclusion of platinum group metals (PGMs) in trade volume calculations despite their exemption from tariffs.

a642.speaker: Minerals Council SA
a642.speech: welcomed the exclusion of PGMs, manganese, coal and gold — which together comprise 76% of South African mineral exports to the US — but warned of broader consequences.

a642.speaker: Hugo Pienaar, chief economist at the Minerals Council SA
a642.speech: “Despite the exclusions, we remain concerned about the adverse impact on sentiment and global growth. Even PGMs are not immune. Tariffs on vehicles mean fewer sales, which hits demand for autocatalysts.”

a642.speaker: Mzila Mthenjane, Minerals Council CEO
a642.speech: “Trade wars are bad for everyone. Even exempt sectors suffer from slower global growth. And when growth contracts, so does demand — even for metals we think are protected.”

a642.speaker: Parks Tau, Minister of Trade and Industry
a642.speech: “It is a sector that could be affected internationally … [these tariffs] expose concentration risks and challenge our beneficiation strategies.”

a642.speaker: White House fact sheet
a642.speech: issued on Wednesday to explain the tariff increases, said: “For decades, South Africa has imposed animal health restrictions that are not scientifically justified on US pork products, permitting a very limited list of US pork exports to enter South Africa. South Africa also heavily restricts US poultry exports through high tariffs, anti-dumping duties, and unjustified animal health restrictions. These barriers have contributed to a 78% decline in US poultry exports to South Africa, from $89-million in 2019 to $19-million in 2024.”

a642.speaker: Dan Halstrom, president and CEO of the US Meat Export Federation (USMEF)
a642.speech: told Daily Maverick: “President Trump’s executive order definitely provides more clarity on the administration’s approach to reciprocal tariffs, and we appreciate the White House bringing attention to the markets in which US exports face significant trade barriers. USMEF’s main concern is obviously how our trading partners will react. We are hopeful that they will focus on eliminating barriers to trade rather than imposing restrictive countermeasures.”

a642.speaker: US poultry industry sources
a642.speech: indicated they were not aware of any outstanding issues on US poultry imports into SA.

a642.speaker: Farmers (South Africa)
a642.speech: are warning of rising input costs just ahead of the next planting season, as a weaker rand has made imports of fuel, fertiliser and agricultural chemicals more expensive.

a686.speaker: Ethiopian government
a686.speech: Insists the new taxes and fees are essential to maintain critical services.

a686.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a686.speech: Predicts inflation will spike to approximately 29pc later this year.

a686.speaker: King Rehoboam (biblical story invoked by many Ethiopians)
a686.speech: "My father laid heavy burdens on you, but I'm going to make them even heavier!"

a686.speaker: Mamo Mihretu, Central Bank Governor of Ethiopia
a686.speech: Set the ambitious target of lowering inflation below 10pc, which appears increasingly unattainable while conflicts and political instability are ongoing.

a908.speaker: Fenella Frost, United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) resident representative
a908.speech: Has called for investment in climate resilience, warning that erratic rainfall, prolonged droughts and pest infestations continue to threaten Malawi’s economic stability; in her remarks during the Post-CoP29 National Climate Change Symposium in Lilongwe she said the challenges undermine the implementation of Malawi 2063, the country’s long-term development strategy ; “Malawi must take a strategic approach to ensure investment in key areas such as capacity building for resource mobilisation and utilisation.”

a908.speaker: Fiona Ritchie, British High Commissioner
a908.speech: Said donor fatigue and aid freezes require Malawi to rethink its approach to climate financing: “Public finance will not suffice, especially in a world with constrained foreign aid. Private financing will be key to freeing up resources to invest in Malawi’s resilience to climate change.”

a908.speaker: Owen Chomanika, Minister of Natural Resources and Climate Change
a908.speech: Reaffirmed the government’s commitment to securing climate funds through strategic partnerships.

a908.speaker: Malawi and fellow Least Developed Countries (LDCs) at CoP29
a908.speech: Requested $1 trillion in climate financing at CoP29 in Baku, Azerbaijan in November last year.

a1073.speaker: Government of Liberia
a1073.speech: Says it has initiated some fiscal rules as a strategy that will help the country amid the USAID support drawdown.

a1073.speaker: Augustine Ngafuan, Finance Minister of Liberia
a1073.speech: Named the reduction of allowances of government officials, among others, as the steps taken; according to the minister of finance, the USAID drawdown is a shock to Liberia, but it is not a doom for the country.

a1073.speaker: Augustine Ngafuan, Finance Minister of Liberia
a1073.speech: Placed both the internal and external debt stock at two billion US dollars, with a little over one billion USD for internal debt, and added that Liberia's integrity is being restored gradually because the government has been making payments through the national budget.

a1080.speaker: Zimbabwe police
a1080.speech: Said hundreds of children were abused at the church's farm; said that 251 minors were found living on a farm run by Chokurongerwa outside Harare during a raid carried out earlier this week ; the children "were being used to perform various physical activities for the benefit of the sect's leadership," police said ; they did not go to school but were instead being "taught life skills" and "subjected to abuse as cheap labour."

a1080.speaker: Zimbabwean authorities
a1080.speech: Said "Self-styled prophet" Ishmael Chokurongerwa, 56, was arrested on Tuesday alongside seven congregants "for criminal activities which include abuse of minors."

a1080.speaker: Paul Nyathi, police spokesperson
a1080.speech: Told AFP that church members were also denied access to medicine and healthcare.

a1080.speaker: Former church member (anonymous), interviewed by a local radio station
a1080.speech: Said Chokurongerwa was keeping hundreds of families at his farm which was blocked from the outside world. The woman said the shrine was named Canaan and sect members believed that the world was coming to an end.

a1113.speaker: United States government (own figures)
a1113.speech: According to their own figures, the United States spent $72 billion on foreign aid in 2023, of which more than $40 billion was administered by USAID. That year, the largest sector of all foreign aid was "economic development", with $19.4 billion, most of which went to Ukraine.

a1113.speaker: Theo Acheampong, economist and political risk analyst
a1113.speech: Argues that strategic investments, fairer trade and concessional financing — not aid — will bring structural economic change in developing countries.

a1113.speaker: International Energy Agency
a1113.speech: According to the International Energy Agency, 600 million people, or 43% of the total population, have no access to electricity, the majority of them living in sub-Saharan Africa.

a1320.speaker: First responders in Gaza
a1320.speech: Said their operations were at a near standstill, more than two months into a full Israeli blockade that has left food and fuel in severe shortage.

a1320.speaker: Israel
a1320.speech: Denies a humanitarian crisis is unfolding in the Gaza Strip, where it plans to expand military operations to force Hamas to free hostages held there since the group's October 2023 attack.

a1320.speaker: Mahmud Bassal, spokesman for the civil defence agency
a1320.speech: "Seventy-five percent of our vehicles have stopped operating due to a lack of diesel fuel." ; Added that its teams, who play a critical role as first responders in the Gaza Strip, were also facing a "severe shortage of electricity generators and oxygen devices."

a1320.speaker: UN agencies and other humanitarian organisations
a1320.speech: Have warned for weeks of dwindling supplies of everything from fuel and medicine to food and clean water in the coastal territory that is home to 2.4 million Palestinians.

a1320.speaker: UNICEF, the UN's agency for children
a1320.speech: Warned that Gaza's children face "a growing risk of starvation, illness and death" after UN-supported kitchens shut down due to lack of food supplies.

a1320.speaker: Over 20 independent experts mandated by the UN's Human Rights Council
a1320.speech: Demanded action on Wednesday to avert the "annihilation" of Palestinians in Gaza.

a1320.speaker: Moamen al-Eid, Palestinian waiting in line to donate blood
a1320.speech: "In these difficult circumstances, we have come to support the injured and sick, amid severe food shortages and a lack of proteins, by donating blood."

a1320.speaker: Hind Joba, laboratory head at the field hospital in Khan Yunis
a1320.speech: "There is no food or drink, the crossings are closed, and there is no access to nutritious or protein-rich food." ; "Still, people responded to the call, fulfilling their humanitarian duty by donating blood," despite the toll on their own bodies ; "But this blood is vital, and they know that every drop helps save the life of an injured."

a1320.speaker: Israeli security official (anonymous)
a1320.speech: Stated that a "window" remained for negotiations on the release of hostages until the end of US president Donald Trump's visit to the Gulf, scheduled from 13 May to 16.

a1320.speaker: Hamas
a1320.speech: Is demanding a "comprehensive and complete agreement" to end the war, and on Wednesday denounced what it called Israel's attempt to impose a "partial" deal.

a1320.speaker: Gaza civil defence agency
a1320.speech: Said air strikes at dawn killed at least eight people.

a1320.speaker: AFP tally based on official data
a1320.speech: Put at 1,218 the number of people killed on the Israeli side, mostly civilians, in Hamas's 7 October 2023 attack on southern Israel.

a1320.speaker: Hamas-run Health Ministry (data)
a1320.speech: Reported that the Israeli offensive launched in retaliation for the 7 October attack has killed at least 52,653 people in Gaza, mostly civilians; the ministry's data is considered reliable by the UN.

a1320.speaker: AFP journalist
a1320.speech: Reported that on Thursday, Palestinians waited in line to donate blood at a field hospital in Gaza's southern city of Khan Yunis.

a1359.speaker: Jean Pierre-Rousseau, Project Director, Winrock International
a1359.speech: Has said that the USAID Feed the Future Agricultural Extension and Advisory Service Activity, being implemented in the seven focal States in Nigeria has facilitated the in-flow of N67billion to smallholder farmers in the last four years. He explained that over two million farmers have benefited from the USAID initiative, which has facilitated the inflow of over N67 billion to smallholder farmers in Benue, Cross River, Delta, Ebonyi, Kaduna, Kebbi, and Niger States. He said over 311 MSMEs have been raised, who serve as change catalysts, by bringing innovation, information, and productivity enhancing inputs and services to the doorsteps of over two million smallholder farmers in the seven focal states. ; "I have had the privilege of working with the Extension Activity since its inception five years ago. In designing this initiative, we faced the challenge of finding effective solutions to deliver impactful extension services that improve the livelihoods, productivity, profitability and market access of over 2 million smallholder farmers across Benue, Cross River, Delta, Ebonyi, Kaduna, Kebbi, and Niger states. I know this is a challenge familiar to everyone in this room. How do we transform agriculture in Nigeria to achieve food sufficiency, particularly when our extension system relies on one extension agent serving 10,000 farmers? The heart of our solution lies in Nigeria's remarkable spirit of entrepreneurship. The Extension Activity, alongside our partners at the Federal Department of Agriculture Extension, has harnessed this spirit to transform extension services. I am proud to stand in front of you this morning and announce that today we have over 311 micro, small and medium enterprises—MSMEs—serving as change catalysts, by bringing innovation, information, and productivity enhancing inputs and services to the doorstep of over 2 million smallholder farmers. The entrepreneurship, ingenuity and innovation coming from those MSMEs, many of which have joined us today, have demonstrated to the nation how Private Sector Extension service delivered through MSMEs has a catalytic impact on national food security. These MSME change agents have transformed extension services from mere information dissemination into a robust enterprise. They have showcased the positive economic and social benefits of private sector investments in smallholder-oriented service provision. This not only increases the revenue of MSMEs but also promotes productivity and prosperity among smallholder farmers. Those MSMEs have built the business case that investment in on-farm service provision linked to market opportunity is a profitable enterprise. You will hear testimonies today directly from the Feed the Future Extension Activity MSME partners about how this investment has translated to increased sales and profitability. You will hear about how they have exponentially increased their farmer customer base for improved climate resilient seed, fertilizer, mechanization services amongst 39 other MIPs: most impactful practices." ; "By providing market-aligned and market responsive business solutions, or most impactful practices, to smallholder farmers we have been able to realize farmer adoption rates of promoted practices and technologies of upwards of 70%. MSMEs have also been critical intermediaries for facilitating the flow of affordable financing to smallholder farmers. Finance they need to invest in improving their productivity to capture new market opportunity. Through those MSMEs we have rolled out input credit models that have generated over 95% repayment rates, and facilitated the flow of over 67 billion Naira in financing to smallholder farmers." ; He expressed confidence that Nigeria can become a powerhouse of innovation in smallholder service delivery, adding that "Together through collaboration between government, private sector, and donor programmes, we can achieve transformative impacts on livelihoods."

a1359.speaker: Dr. Ben Odoemena, Chief of Party, USAID Feed the Future Agricultural Extension and Advisory Services Activity in Nigeria
a1359.speech: In his presentation, said the Extension Activity's approach is anchored on private sector engagement, with a primary focus on partnering with MSMEs and other private sector extension and market service providers to test, adapt and scale MIPs for smallholder farmers. Odoemena affirmed that MIPs are business solutions/opportunities that effectively and sustainably facilitate access to agro-inputs, market and extension messaging by smallholder farmers.

a1359.speaker: Farmers benefiting from the USAID initiative (testimonies)
a1359.speech: Shared testimonies and success stories about how they have increased their customer base, incomes and livelihoods through the implementation of the USAID initiative in collaboration with the Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security.

a1479.speaker: Economic experts and analysts (unnamed)
a1479.speech: say the Malawi government has done well in ending the Extended Credit Facility (ECF) loan programme with the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

a1479.speaker: Betchani Tchereni, Secretary to the Treasury for economic affairs
a1479.speech: said some of the IMF's conditions were that government should lay off some workers, should not increase salaries, and should not recruit people in various sectors ; added that although the government has been following good economic management policies, the country has faced various problems such as drought, cholera and cyclones, which have damaged the country's economy ; says people should not worry about this matter because the government has put in place good policies and plans to help the country's economy move forward.

a1479.speaker: Benedicto Kondowe, head of the Civil Society Advocacy Forum
a1479.speech: said what the government has done is proper because it is considering the welfare of the people of this country, who would suffer if it followed all of the IMF's conditions ; said the time has come for the government to continue to stand firm by following and finding good policies that do not depend on loans and on financial assistance from institutions and wealthy countries ; gave the example of what the American government has done in shutting down some of its agencies such as USAID, which had been providing various forms of assistance to developing countries such as Malawi.

a1577.speaker: US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA Fisheries)
a1577.speech: Granted Morocco official recognition confirming the compliance of its fisheries with the requirements of the Marine Mammal Protection Act, ensuring the continuity of Moroccan seafood exports to the United States from January 2026 to December 2029.

a1577.speaker: Moroccan Secretariat of State for Maritime Fisheries (official statement)
a1577.speech: Announced the decision and stated that all Moroccan fisheries listed on the list of foreign fisheries were found to comply with American standards, following a thorough review of the application submitted by Rabat, and that this recognition attests to the "level of maturity reached by public policies in the preservation of marine resources," notably through the adoption of sustainable management measures and rigorous controls.

a1577.speaker: Moroccan authorities
a1577.speech: Believe that this decision consolidates the confidence of international consumers and importers in the Kingdom's products, while strengthening its competitiveness against the sector's major global players.

a1669.speaker: José Tonato, Minister of Living Environment and Infrastructure, in charge of Sustainable Development (Benin)
a1669.speech: Said the ambition by 2040 is for Benin's forest areas to be better managed for their multiple functions.

a1669.speaker: Representative of Sweden, financial partner on the project
a1669.speech: "We hope that this project will be implemented successfully for the well-being of the communities."

a1669.speaker: Ange Obama, FAO Resident Representative
a1669.speech: Said that wetland forests constitute an important source of fuel and food but are extremely affected by degradation, meaning that the implementation of specific actions under the project 'Global Forest Transformation for People and Climate: Focus on West Africa' will benefit communities and contribute to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

a1944.speaker: Centre for Democracy and Economic Development Initiatives (CDEDI) (statement)
a1944.speech: Has issued a statement accusing Cabinet ministers, top government officials, and the ruling elite of capturing Malawi's economy and exploiting the disparity between the official and black market exchange rates for personal gain.

a1944.speaker: Sylvester Namiwa, CDEDI Executive Officer
a1944.speech: Said this has led to a further weakening of the local currency against the US dollar, with the powerful individuals accessing foreign exchange from commercial banks and the Reserve Bank of Malawi (RBM) under false pretences, only to sell it on the black market at inflated rates. "Malawians may wish to know that at the height of this forex crisis, a senior Cabinet minister and influential Malawi Congress Party figure, whose name we have but will withhold for now, has the luxury of buying real property in US dollars." ; "Just recently, the flamboyant politician applied for $450,000 at one of the commercial banks, which is about K788 million at the official rate, but took the money directly to a Malawian businessperson of Asian origin, where he sold the dollars at K4,200, translating to about K1.8 billion, making an instant profit of almost K1 billion."

a1944.speaker: Sylvester Namiwa, CDEDI Executive Officer
a1944.speech: Condemned this "illicit business" and called on Malawians to stand up against it, saying as per the wording and spirit of Section 12 of the Republican Constitution, Malawians should not feel helpless or intimidated, rather they should stand up to address the crisis that is threatening their survival. "By the end of the day, Malawians will be allowed to distinguish between honest and corrupt public officials," he added. "It is sad to note that after voting, Malawians have nothing that gives them leverage to invoke the powers contained in the Constitution."

a1944.speaker: Centre for Democracy and Economic Development Initiatives (CDEDI)
a1944.speech: Has launched an initiative dubbed "The People Power Forum" to expose those involved in this corruption and to give back power to the people; the organization is urging Malawians within and outside the country, groups and institutions to come forward and provide both technical and material support.

a1970.speaker: Euphrasie Kouassi Yao, holder of the UNESCO Chair on Water, Women and Decision-Making Power (Cuefpod) and initiator of the Crea-Paix programme
a1970.speech: “We have heard the cry of our brothers and sisters in Goma. Our vocation is to work for peace and that goes through training, prevention, but also concrete action. This donation, although symbolic, reflects our commitment and our solidarity,” she declared after handing over the envelope; she called on everyone to contribute to this support effort, recalling that “when your brother suffers, it is you who suffer”.

a1970.speaker: Nelly Ouassénan, 2nd Deputy Mayor of Cocody
a1970.speech: Stressed the importance of a collective awareness in the face of the tragedy unfolding in Goma: “This donation is more than aid, it is a message of hope, a testimony of our commitment,” she insisted, recalling the support of the Cocody municipal council for the victims.

a1970.speaker: Marie Noëlle Koyara, coordinator of the Network for Rethinking Security in Africa (Rras)
a1970.speech: Called for solidarity, thinking of displaced families and the wandering children who are victims of the conflict: “We cannot change everything in one day, however we can start today. Every action counts,” she affirmed.

a1976.speaker: White House Office of Management and Budget
a1976.speech: Announced the decision to cut $5bn in foreign aid already allocated by Congress in a social media post on Friday.

a1976.speaker: White House (statement)
a1976.speech: "The Trump Administration is committed to getting America's fiscal house in order by cutting government spending that is woke, weaponised, and wasteful."

a1976.speaker: Government Accountability Office
a1976.speech: Has questioned the legality of pocket rescissions, arguing the budget tool bypasses Congress's power of the purse.

a1976.speaker: Senator Susan Collins, Republican from Maine
a1976.speech: Said the Constitution "makes clear that Congress has the responsibility for the power of the purse" and any effort to claw back funds "without congressional approval is a clear violation of the law" ; said in a statement: "Instead of this attempt to undermine the law, the appropriate way is to identify ways to reduce excessive spending through the bipartisan, annual appropriations process. Congress approves rescissions regularly as part of this process."

a1976.speaker: Chuck Schumer, Senate Democratic Leader, of New York
a1976.speech: Said that Trump's use of the pocket rescission could undermine normal congressional procedure and result in "a painful and entirely unnecessary shutdown" of the government.

a1976.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a1976.speech: Has largely shuttered the US Agency for International Development (USAID) because he found its spending "wasteful."

a1979.speaker: Kwaku Sintim Misa (KSM), Ghanaian comedian and filmmaker
a1979.speech: Has revealed that his biggest breakthrough as an actor was landing a role in the acclaimed US television series Law & Order: "In the US, I got some mileage in film and in acting. I acted in a very popular series called, Law and Order, which I think was my biggest deal because that series was one of the highly rated primetime shows in the US. To appear on it, was a biggest deal."

a1979.speaker: Kwaku Sintim Misa (KSM), Ghanaian comedian and filmmaker
a1979.speech: Speaking on the Career Trail program on Joy Learning TV and Joy News, shared that acting was something he had been drawn to from a very young age: "It's very interesting because as long as I remember, I wanted to act. I don't know what I saw in acting. I remember back in the day my eldest brother went to study in the UK and I remember writing to him, asking him to find a school in the UK for me to come and act" ; "Anytime I went out and I came back, I had a story. I always had imagination, so anytime I came back, I had a story. Sometimes, I will say, 'this is what I'm going to tell them when I get home'. The funny thing is my family used to tag me as a 'liar'. Interestingly, that was the beginning of a writer."

a1979.speaker: Kwaku Sintim Misa (KSM), Ghanaian comedian and filmmaker
a1979.speech: On his training: "I went to the university, it was all about Threatre Arts. After high school, I went to NAFTI for 1 year before travelling to the US. We were the pioneers of NAFTI" ; on his first film role: "When I returned to Ghana during a summer break, one of my friends from NAFTI was shooting a film and featured me in it. That was my first film experience, and I truly enjoyed it."

a1979.speaker: Kwaku Sintim Misa (KSM), Ghanaian comedian and filmmaker
a1979.speech: Highlighted his groundbreaking achievement as the first African to perform an original one-man show in the US, Thoughts of a Confused Black Man: "I was the first African to have done an original one-man play on Broadway."

a1979.speaker: Kwaku Sintim Misa (KSM), Ghanaian comedian and filmmaker
a1979.speech: Urged young people to pay close attention to their natural talents: "I always tell people, anything you can do that comes without effort most likely is your talent. There are people like that, you teach them computers, they just sit behind it, they know what they are doing. Whatever they do, they do it effortlessly. And I tell people take a note of that. If you can do anything without major effort but at the same time excel, most likely is your talent. So pay attention to that" ; emphasised that talent is not confined to the creative arts: "The other mistake that people make is that they think that talent is referred to the arts, like singing, dancing, acting, and painting. It is not true. You can be a talented mathematician, architect, chemist because it comes to you effortlessly. Don't limit talent to the creative arts alone. Talent is broad and everyone has a talent."

a2006.speaker: David Adeleke (Davido), music star
a2006.speech: Speaking during an interview with music executive Bankulli, the Grammy nominee said he regrets his hard work, noting that he has billions of dollars waiting for him if he decides not to work again. He stated that the odds against him are why he is still working ; “I’m grateful to myself for being hardworking. The individual strength and mental ability that goes into this type of work, especially with a lot of odds against me, then I say I have to do it. It’s not for the money; I have billions of dollars waiting for me. Even if I don’t work again in my life, I have billions of dollars. But I’m working because I love my job.”

a2035.speaker: Harold Jiya, NBM plc chief executive officer
a2035.speech: Said Malawi is currently importing approximately 20 000 metric tonnes (MT) of bananas annually costing about $4 million (about K7.1 billion), and that the dependence on imports not only constrains the country's economy and foreign currency, but also reflects the gap in local production ; "Mulanje and Thyolo were dominant in banana production in the 1980s and 1990s. You might not know this, but the banana bunchy top virus, which struck in 2004, reduced banana plantations significantly in these districts, leading to reliance on imports." ; said the reduction of banana output in the two districts brought in dependency on handouts.

a2035.speaker: Harold Jiya, NBM plc chief executive officer
a2035.speech: "It is our hope that the support to these demonstration plots will help to build these communities and eventually these districts will be able to produce more bananas." ; said the main objective of the demonstration farms, also known as smart farms, is to revive banana farming in these two districts on a commercial scale and further build up communities to be self-reliant ; "We not only affirm our support to the project, but also to lay the foundation for sustainable growth that empowers our farmers, uplifts their families and revitalises the nation's economic fabric. Let me add that this partnership stems from the recognition of a critical challenge that has affected Malawi's agricultural industry for two decades."

a2035.speaker: MacLeod Nkhoma, Centre for Agricultural Transformation (CAT) executive director
a2035.speech: Described the partnership with NBM plc as a significant milestone that will support smallholder banana farmers, and said that through the partnership CAT will provide technical agricultural support to help farmers boost productivity through the demonstration plots in the two districts, with each district having one smart farm ; "The bank, in turn, will provide crucial financial backing to further this effort. This partnership between Land O'Lakes Venture37-CAT and the National Bank of Malawi is a clear demonstration of our shared commitment to improving banana production and productivity in Mulanje and Thyolo districts." ; said land for the demonstration plots in both districts has been secured and they are ready to begin work this growing season.

a2149.speaker: Junior Nelson, town chief of Back Camp
a2149.speech: "The roofing of these toilets, made possible by USAID's support, will stop people from defecating in the bushes." ; added that the visible progress in roofing has encouraged more residents to purchase "Quee" Toilets, with several households now actively constructing their sanitation facilities thanks to this U.S. Government-backed initiative.

a2149.speaker: 2021 Liberia Sanitation Market Assessment (report)
a2149.speech: According to the assessment, 1.8 million people still practice open defecation, putting their health and that of their children at significant risk.

a2149.speaker: USAID-funded Countywide Sanitation Activity (CWSA) (press release)
a2149.speech: Announced that, as part of the U.S. Government's commitment to improving sanitation and public health in Liberia, CWSA has partnered with African United for Progress (AUP) to provide roofing materials for vulnerable households in Todee District, rural Montserrado County, supporting the USG's larger goal of ending open defecation and ensuring healthier living conditions across Liberia; AUP provided 3,400 square feet of metal roofing sheets valued at USD$29,512 (63% of the total cost) and USAID funded the remaining 37% (US$17,566), completing roofing for 85 households in Back Camp, Yakpazuah Town and Freeman Town over 16 days.

a2149.speaker: Liberia's public health law
a2149.speech: Mandates that every household must build and maintain a toilet.

a2204.speaker: Nigerian presidency (official statement/communiqué)
a2204.speech: According to the statement, Tinubu appointed new ministers for humanitarian aid and poverty reduction, trade and investment, labour and livestock development, as well as deputy ministers for Foreign Affairs, Education and Housing; the ministers of Education, Tourism, Women's Affairs and Youth Development and the deputy minister of Housing were dismissed.

a2298.speaker: Lazarus Chakwera, President of Malawi
a2298.speech: has expressed deep appreciation for the strong bilateral relationship between Malawi and India; his remarks came during a meeting with Indian President Her Excellency Smt. Droupadi Murmu at Kamuzu Palace on Friday.

a2298.speaker: Nancy Tembo, Minister of Foreign Affairs (Malawi)
a2298.speech: updated the media post-meeting, highlighting President Chakwera's gratitude for India's steadfast support across various sectors, including trade, health, education, and military peacekeeping. He also acknowledged India's recent humanitarian assistance. ; "The President is particularly pleased that the Indian President chose Malawi as one of her official visit destinations." ; "He emphasized India's role in supporting least developed countries in multilateral organizations, ensuring they receive fair treatment on the global stage."

a2340.speaker: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a2340.speech: Called for efforts to mobilize more resources in response to an escalating drought crisis in several areas of Somalia and warned that the spread of prolonged, extreme dry conditions is worsening an already dire humanitarian situation ; said the poor performance of the October-to-December 2024 deyr (short) rains led to drought conditions in southern and central regions and the current hot and dry conditions ; "Given that drought conditions worsened progressively through January, immediate humanitarian assistance and long-term resilience interventions, including borehole drilling, livestock support, and sustainable water management, are urgently required" ; warned that food insecurity, malnutrition and displacement would worsen in the coming months, disproportionately affecting women, children and marginalized groups ; said an estimated 4.4 million people are facing high levels of acute food insecurity, with 1.6 million children likely to suffer from acute malnutrition through July ; said drier conditions will increase competition over resources, strain coping mechanisms and heighten risks for disease outbreaks.

a2340.speaker: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)
a2340.speech: Projected that the April-to-June Gu seasonal rains would be below-normal across most parts of Somalia, with a delayed onset in key agricultural areas.

a2387.speaker: Rumbidzai, sex worker from Epworth, Harare (middle name used only)
a2387.speech: “I don’t want to die — my children are still young. Who will take care of them?” ; “If anything, Trump should lighten his heart, because our lives are hanging by a thread.”

a2387.speaker: Rumbidzai, sex worker from Epworth, Harare (middle name used only)
a2387.speech: “Local clinics only give us three to four strips per week. In our trade, that’s not enough. People will take risks when supplies run out — something we desperately want to avoid.”

a2387.speaker: Donald Trump, US President (directive)
a2387.speech: A recent directive ordering the United States Agency for International Development to cease operations has led to the shutdown of numerous crucial programmes in Zimbabwe, directly impacting organisations such as Population Solutions for Health and CeSHHAR which have long been a lifeline to sex workers.

a2387.speaker: Chipo, outreach worker serving sex worker communities since 2015 (middle name used only)
a2387.speech: “The sex workers are crying; they are afraid of dying” ; says that in Harare alone mobile clinics are serving nearly 6 000 sex workers — all now left scrambling for basic health care.

a2387.speaker: Beauty Magora, former sex worker and community mobiliser
a2387.speech: Is worried about her upcoming HIV prevention treatment, which she typically receives as pre-exposure prophylaxis every two months free of charge through mobile clinics, and is uncertain about switching to tablet medication: “I don’t know if there will be any effects if I switch to tablets,” she says.

a2387.speaker: Muchanyara Cynthia Mukamuri, chairperson of the Women’s Coalition of Zimbabwe
a2387.speech: Says a shortage of condoms will lead to the creation of a breeding ground for infections and reinfections, affecting not just sex workers but their clients as well.

a2387.speaker: Muchanyara Cynthia Mukamuri, chairperson of the Women’s Coalition of Zimbabwe
a2387.speech: Adds that a huge portion of funding for antiretroviral therapy came from the US: “If that is withdrawn, will Zimbabwe be able to cope with the rise of need for HIV prevention, treatment and all these things?” ; emphasizes that with all the natural resources Zimbabwe possesses, the country should now strive for self-sufficiency: “We need to revisit our strategies, refocus our efforts, and redirect our resources to ensure that people living with HIV are not left at the mercy of whoever decides to provide — or withhold — resources,” she says.

a2506.speaker: Martha Molete, Cancer Association of South Africa (CANSA)
a2506.speech: "One in every 31 women are diagnosed with cervical cancer in her lifetime and it kills over 3 400 women in South Africa each year."

a2506.speaker: Martha Molete, Cancer Association of South Africa (CANSA)
a2506.speech: According to Molete, the vaccine could save hundreds of thousands of lives and could eradicate cervical cancer in time.

a2506.speaker: Dr Navin Singh, Medical Director of GSK
a2506.speech: "The decision to approve GSK's cervical cancer vaccine represents a great step forward for all South African women. Physicians will now have access to this important vaccine to help protect women against this disease."

a2506.speaker: Cancer Association of South Africa (CANSA) (prepared statement)
a2506.speech: CANSA believes that the cervical cancer vaccine should be made compulsory for all girls and boys in South Africa: "The current price of the vaccine is around R700 and three shots are required, therefore it would cost R2100 to have one person vaccinated. It is estimated that about 300 000 South Africans should be vaccinated every year, adding up to a cost of R630 million per annum."

a2506.speaker: Cancer Association of South Africa (CANSA) (document prepared for Finance Minister Trevor Manuel)
a2506.speech: Suggested that an increased tax on tobacco could cover the costs of vaccination.

a2506.speaker: World Health Organization (WHO) and International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC)
a2506.speech: Pap smears are currently the recommended method of screening, according to the WHO and the IARC.

a2506.speaker: Medical Research Council
a2506.speech: According to the Medical Research Council, although cervical cancer is a preventable disease that is curable if detected and treated in its early stages, it remains the leading cause of cancer-related deaths in South African women.

a2558.speaker: Jessica Mubanga, hairdresser in Lusaka's Emmasdale residential area
a2558.speech: “Contraceptives are dangerous to women's health and they can harm your womb. In fact, most of my female friends have gained weight as a result of contraceptive pills use. I will never use them.”

a2558.speaker: Lydia, workmate of Jessica Mubanga (surname not given)
a2558.speech: “Yes, you are absolutely right boi (my friend), my neighbour has lost shape ever since she started using contraceptive pills. Besides, I hear family planning methods such as injectables and implants cause cancer and infertility.”

a2558.speaker: World Health Organisation (WHO) (statistics)
a2558.speech: According to statistics by the World Health Organisation, about 214 million women in developing countries such as Zambia wish to avoid pregnancy but are not using modern contraceptives due to negative myths and misconceptions about them.

a2558.speaker: Maternal health experts
a2558.speech: Say that family planning is not only safe but has a positive influence on reducing the incidence of unintended pregnancies, unplanned births, and maternal mortality.

a2558.speaker: Dr. Annabel Mulonda, consultant obstetrician and gynaecologist
a2558.speech: Explained that contrary to the negative myths and misconceptions, family planning such as oral contraceptive pills and implants are very safe with no scientific evidence of causing cancer: “Family planning such as hormonal methods or even permanent methods such as tubal ligation and vasectomy are very safe. They do not cause any harm to humans' health” ; stated that access to family planning information and services prevents unnecessary maternal death or illness due to an unintended pregnancy, and emphasized that women who choose family planning are healthier and face a lower risk of dying during pregnancy and childbirth.

a2558.speaker: Dr. Annabel Mulonda, consultant obstetrician and gynaecologist
a2558.speech: Reiterated that women do not gain or lose weight as a result of contraceptive pills use: “A woman's weight may fluctuate naturally due to changes in age or lifestyle. But because changes in weight are common, women wrongly attribute their natural weight gain or loss to the use of pills” ; explained that after contraceptive pills are swallowed they dissolve in the digestive system just like any food or medicine without accumulating anywhere in the body: “After they produce their contraceptive effect, the hormones in the pills are metabolised in the liver and gut and are then eliminated from the body. In fact, each pill lasts for about 24 hours in the woman's body and does not get stuck anywhere. That is why pills are taken every day, preferably at the same time, to be effective” ; urged those experiencing weight gain to be active and control their diets: “Maintaining shape and avoiding gaining weight can be achieved through exercising regularly and controlling diets. Otherwise, the benefits of family planning are many for women, men and children.”

a2558.speaker: Professor Wilbroad Mutale, professor of public health and medicine, chief executive officer and founder of Teledoctor Zambia
a2558.speech: Said family planning does not make a person infertile but rather works in a way that stops them from getting pregnant until the desired time when they are ready; said contraceptives do not cause infertility regardless of how long they are taken, and that women who stop using contraceptives can become pregnant again as long as they have not reached menopause ; advised those who are not comfortable with hormonal methods to choose from the various types of family planning methods that suit them: “Family planning is not just about taking pills or injections, there are various types of family planning methods. Depending on their choice, couples or women can decide the type of family planning methods they intend to use. If they are not comfortable to use hormonal methods, they can for example, use natural method” ; said that with family planning women can have children by choice and not by chance, thereby reducing the rate of unintended pregnancies and the need for unsafe abortions; noted that family planning gives women enough space between pregnancies for their body to completely recover from the effects of pregnancy, labour and childbirth; and said several couples in the developing world like European countries are using a modern method of contraception for healthy timing, spacing and limiting of births to achieve their desired family size.

a2558.speaker: Mrs. Getrude Nyambe, 42, mother of four, resident of Lusaka's Matero Township
a2558.speech: Testified that before having access to family planning information and services her life was not stable as she suffered from the physical and mental toll of pregnancies, but that her life took a positive turn when she embraced modern contraceptives; narrated that she was initially hesitant because of myths and misconceptions: “I initially never wanted to use contraceptives because of the strong rumour that they cause cancer. I was also scared that I would gain a lot of weight and experience heavy menstruation. But here I am, my shape has not changed” ; said one of her cousins, a nurse at Matero Level One Hospital, encouraged her to practice family planning after explaining the benefits; said embracing family planning has paid off as it has helped ensure the wellbeing of her family and that she and her husband have managed to maintain a small family: “Had it not been for embracing family planning, I would have about seven children by now and fail to take good care of them. Using contraceptive injection has been a game changer for me in the sense that it has helped my husband and I to give our four children the best in life, especially good education and nutrition because we have a manageable number of children.”

a2558.speaker: Mrs. Judith Tembo, 30, Matero resident
a2558.speech: Disclosed that the implant family planning method has helped her to avoid a mistimed pregnancy, allowing her to further upgrade herself in terms of education: “For me, I have never experienced any health challenge ever since I started using implant family planning method some three years ago when my son was two years and he is now five years. I even enrolled pursuing my Master's degree at the university last year and will be finishing my programme end of this year” ; encouraged her fellow women to ignore the negative myths and misconceptions about family planning, and embrace it if they are to live a health and fulfilling life.

a2558.speaker: Ministry of Health of Zambia
a2558.speech: According to the Ministry of Health in Zambia, family planning is a key component of national development, with a focus on increasing access to a wide range of contraceptive methods through an integrated family planning costed implementation plan (CIP) aiming to significantly raise the contraceptive prevalence rate from 49 percent to 80 percent by the year 2026.

a2558.speaker: Dr Elijah Muchima, Minister of Health of Zambia
a2558.speech: Said the Zambian government is committed to improving family planning services through strategic initiatives, including expanding service delivery points, introducing new contraceptive methods, and enhancing education and counselling programmes; speaking during the opening of the Sexual Reproductive Health Alliance Conference in Lusaka, acknowledged the progress made in increasing contraceptive prevalence rates, reducing unintended pregnancies and improving maternal health outcomes, but noted that challenges in accessing contraceptives remained a significant barrier in the country.

a2558.speaker: Zambia Demographic and Health Survey (2024 ZDHS report)
a2558.speech: According to the latest Zambia Demographic and Health Survey report, contraceptive prevalence is 55 percent among currently married women and 50 percent among sexually active unmarried women; the 2024 ZDHS report indicates that 53 percent of currently married women in Zambia use modern contraceptives, with injectables at 28 percent, implants 11 percent and pills at 6 percent being the most commonly used, and further reveals that 34 percent of sexually active unmarried women have an unmet need for family planning.

a2593.speaker: Professor Babafemi Badejo, scholar and diplomat
a2593.speech: Has championed the inadequacy of the UN ECA-led Quadruple Nexus orientation by pointing out the situational foundation of governance, external dynamics, institutions, and resources, to arrive at the need for the focus to be encompassing by adding these situational foundation concerns to arrive at the Situational Quadruple Nexus (SQN) Analysis.

a2593.speaker: Professor Babafemi Badejo, scholar and diplomat
a2593.speech: Has continued to remain vocal on the need to reduce corruption and the theft of national patrimony as part of the larger problem of leadership deficit.

a2604.speaker: Government of Mozambique (the Executive)
a2604.speech: Says it intends, with the change to the decree governing the Northern Integrated Development Agency (ADIN), to clarify ADIN’s attributions and competences, with regard to institutional coordination and articulation.

a2604.speaker: Decree approved by the Council of Ministers (32nd session)
a2604.speech: According to the approved Decree, ADIN will now carry out the supervision and technical coordination of the implementation of all Sector and Partner Development Programmes and Projects, as well as the articulation of stakeholders in the development of the Northern Region.

a2604.speaker: Council of Ministers of Mozambique (32nd Ordinary Session decisions)
a2604.speech: Approved the Decree extending for a further 90 days the transition period of resources from the Compact II Development Office to the MCA-Mozambique, in order to conclude administrative processes, closure and installation of the institutions; approved a Decree repealing Decree No. 68/2010 on the Mphanda Nkuwa Hydroelectric Project concession; approved the National Strategy for Financial Inclusion for 2025-2031 and a Decree creating the 2025-2031 National Committee for Financial Inclusion; approved the Regulation of Public Water Distribution and Wastewater Drainage Systems; and approved the reappointment of Suzana Loforte for a second term as Chairwoman of the Board of Directors of the Water Regulatory Authority (AURA).

a2659.speaker: Dr Abdoul-Wahab bin Soulaiman al-Djibab, head of the medical mission of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre
a2659.speech: According to the head of the medical mission, the activities and programmes of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre, created in 2015, have extended to around 150 countries. In a brief speech, he expressed his thanks and gratitude to the government and people of Djibouti for the warm welcome, stressing that the voluntary medical campaign for specialised surgery had allowed nearly 100 paediatric urology operations.

a2659.speaker: Fatima al-Sheikh, Resident Representative of the United Nations Development Programme in Djibouti
a2659.speech: Spoke of the humanitarian and relief role of the King Salman Centre, particularly in the Republic of Djibouti, stressing that this institution has become one of the world's leading organisations in terms of humanitarian support to many countries around the world. She also referred in her address to the fruitful partnership existing between the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre and the United Nations Development Programme and their cooperation in supporting developing countries and those suffering from crises and conflicts.

a2659.speaker: Moumin Hassan Barreh, Minister of Muslim Affairs, Culture and Waqf Property of Djibouti
a2659.speech: In his speech, praised the role played by the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre since its creation nearly five years ago. He stressed that the voluntary medical campaign of specialised surgery carried out by this centre in Djibouti reflects the good fraternal relations and the ties existing between Djibouti and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.

a2659.speaker: Minister of Health of Djibouti
a2659.speech: Recalled in his speech that the Saudi medical mission had been able to cover more than 300 patients presenting genito-urinary malformations, 99 of whom were operated on at the Peltier General Hospital.

a2665.speaker: Spokeswoman for the UN refugee agency, UNHCR
a2665.speech: "While we are still assessing the impact of the new US administration's decision, including possible exceptions, we are implementing a series of temporary precautionary measures to mitigate the impact of this funding uncertainty."

a2665.speaker: The Guardian (British newspaper)
a2665.speech: Earlier reported that UNHCR head Filippo Grandi had sent an email that instructed staff to temporarily halt recruitment and international travel ; reported that Mr Grandi also halted orders of new supplies, except when needed for emergency assistance.

a2665.speaker: UNHCR
a2665.speech: The UNHCR refused to comment on the email.

a2665.speaker: US State Department
a2665.speech: Announced the temporary freeze of foreign aid on Sunday.

a2672.speaker: Maitre Joseph Djogbenou, Beninese lawyer
a2672.speech: Warned: "What has changed between ICC and the RAMU is that this time the President of the Republic places himself beside the Minister of Health, but hastens to specify that the project is rather hers."

a2672.speaker: Experts' report on the RAMU
a2672.speech: At this level too, the experts' report is categorical (that the way the RAMU project is being conducted constitutes a danger for the country).

a2838.speaker: Jospong Group of Companies (JGC)
a2838.speech: has revealed plans to secure US$400 million in funding from the African Export-Import Bank (Afrexim Bank) for comprehensive waste management and rice projects in Lagos State, Nigeria, and Ghana; and plans to source an additional US$50 million for its rice project in Ghana.

a2838.speaker: Noah Gyimah, Jospong Group's Chief Investment Officer
a2838.speech: emphasised the need for broader discussions with Afrexim Bank to support the Group's investment efforts across Africa: "The interesting part of that conversation was the various options they offer, including research and development funding for feasibility studies at accommodating rates."

a2838.speaker: Noah Gyimah, Jospong Group's Chief Investment Officer
a2838.speech: stated: "They expressed great interest in food security and funding options for our rice production business," stressing the need for further conversations with Afrexim Bank's leadership to prioritize key projects, outlining project stages and exploring opportunities for collaboration.

a2838.speaker: Prof. Benedict Oramah, President and Chairman of the Board of Directors at Afreximbank
a2838.speech: "Africa is disproportionately affected by the impacts of global climate change despite being responsible for less than 4% of global emissions. Losses in economic growth, migrations and regional instability represent significant negative impacts of climate change on the continent that will probably intensify in the next decade. We are at the point where taking action does not only suggest good environmental stewardship but must also be seen as a sound economic policy considering that the cost of immediate and decisive action is far less than the cost of inaction and delayed efforts. The issue of financing climate adaptation in Africa and the Island States of the Caribbean has become an emergency and as such our participation at COP29 is an opportunity to advocate for Africa and the Caribbean's climate priorities, amplify their voice in global discussions, and push for urgent climate finance." ; added that financial resources and sound investments are critical to addressing climate change, lowering emissions, encouraging adaptation as well as building resilience, explaining that Africa needs between US$1.3 trillion and US$1.6 trillion in total climate financing every year till 2030 to meet its pressing needs.

a2947.speaker: Ethel Mkandawire, 15-year-old Standard Eight learner at Chitimba Primary School, Chiswankhata Village
a2947.speech: "It was difficult for me to balance school and household chores because I had to wake up around 3 or 4 am to fetch water. I spent most of my morning collecting water, and by the time I got to class, I was already tired, which affected my concentration." ; Says that the maintenance of the borehole allows her to wake up at 3 o'clock in the morning to study rather than to fetch water, which has improved her performance in class: "The construction of the borehole has allowed me to have ample time to prepare for my Standard Eight examinations. The borehole is just a few minutes from my home, so I have plenty of time to study."

a2947.speaker: Princess Chisambo, six-year-old girl from Chiswankhata Village
a2947.speech: Concurs with Ethel, saying the borehole has provided her with the opportunity to drink safe water.

a2947.speaker: Witness Mhango, a mother of eight from Chiswankhata Village
a2947.speech: Says that access to chlorinated water has reduced the incidence of diarrhoea in the village. "Although we sometimes boiled the water we fetched from the river, we were not consistent. Therefore, cases of diarrhoea, including cholera, were high. But since the borehole was repaired, the cases have decreased, which has increased productivity in our households."

a2947.speaker: Elias Duwe, Secretary of the Chiswankhata Water Management Committee
a2947.speech: Says Unicef, with support from BHA, has trained the committee in borehole management to ensure its sustainability. "Each household contributes K500 monthly, which we use to buy spare parts, and with the expertise we gained from Unicef, we are able to perform minor maintenance when needed," Duwe says.

a2947.speaker: Doctor Chimwendo, Water Monitoring Assistant for Rumphi District
a2947.speech: Says Unicef, in partnership with Self Help Africa, with support from BHA, has constructed a total of six boreholes in Rumphi, which have significantly reduced cases of diarrhoea in the district. "In 2022-23, we registered high cases of diarrhoeal diseases, including cholera, but with the construction of the boreholes, the incidence of diarrhoea has significantly decreased in the target areas," Chimwendo says.

a3526.speaker: Government Annual Economic Report, Ministry of Finance and Economic Planning (Malawi)
a3526.speech: “The decline in catch landings by 9.2 percent has resulted in a corresponding decline in per capita fish consumption from 9.65 kilogrammes [kg] in 2023 to 8.5 kg in the year 2024. This shows that the current fish supply does not meet the needs of the growing population of the country,” the report reads; it also shows an increased number of jobs the fisheries sector supported in the year.

a3526.speaker: Department of Fisheries (Malawi)
a3526.speech: Lamented significant paucity of information and data on both fingerling production and table size fish production among most of the private fish farming investments across the country: “As a result, most of the district fisheries offices are unable to adequately record and report on the fish production status of such establishments. This situation culminates to underestimation and therefore undervaluation of the fisheries sector.”

a3526.speaker: Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) research findings
a3526.speech: Research findings by the FAO unveiled an investment model to transform the fisheries sector with potential to impact over 2 million people in the country.

a3526.speaker: Alfred Tsitsi, FAO researcher
a3526.speech: Found cage farming with more potential, having room for investment of $1.1 billion in lake Malawi and the upper Shire, providing jobs to 384 000 people, a transformation he said can impact on 1.8 million people ; further suggested a total of $250 million investment to develop 168 farms of an average of five hectares each across the country with all the districts having production potential at varying levels.

a3544.speaker: Lucia Maxma Welwolie, student advocate and 12th-grade student at Innovation Preparatory Academy International
a3544.speech: Emphasized the importance of educating Liberian youth and students on taxation and its role in national development, and in a speech at the inaugural National Students Tax Day highlighted the origins and significance of NSTD; addressing policymakers, students and educators, emphasized the importance of empowering future leaders with taxation knowledge: “National Students Tax Day is a milestone in empowering us—the future leaders of Liberia—with the knowledge of taxation and its role in nation-building” ; emphasized that through STEP students are not only learning about taxes but are also being empowered to become informed and engaged citizens contributing to Liberia’s development.

a3544.speaker: Lucia Maxma Welwolie, student advocate and 12th-grade student at Innovation Preparatory Academy International
a3544.speech: Urged the relevant authorities to form a technical working group to ensure the comprehensive implementation of STEP in the national curriculum; outlined STEP’s objectives, which include promoting voluntary tax compliance and integrating tax education into Liberia’s national civic curriculum, and called on stakeholders to revisit the 2022 Memorandum of Understanding between the LRA, MoE, and WAEC Liberia to ensure the program’s full implementation across all secondary schools.

a3544.speaker: Lucia Maxma Welwolie, student advocate and 12th-grade student at Innovation Preparatory Academy International
a3544.speech: Proposed the formal recognition of National Students Tax Day as an annual working holiday to amplify its importance and reach across the nation: “Let us rally behind the call to recognize National Students Tax Day as an annual working holiday.”

a3664.speaker: UNAIDS (Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS)
a3664.speech: Warned that new long-acting HIV prevention - and potentially treatment - medicines can help usher in the end of AIDS if corporate and political leaders move quickly and urgently to prioritise access for all low and middle-income countries ; is urging pharmaceutical companies to move faster and ensure "affordable pricing and generic competition" in the market for the new HIV medicines ; its goal is to reach 10 million people with preventative HIV medicine by the end of 2025.

a3664.speaker: Winnie Byanyima, Executive Director of UNAIDS and Under-Secretary-General of the United Nations
a3664.speech: "These new technologies offer us a real shot at ending AIDS by 2030. But it comes with a caveat - only if pharmaceutical companies, governments, international partners and civil society unite around an HIV prevention and treatment revolution, can we use these medicines to their full potential and end AIDS much sooner than we previously thought." ; "We have no problem with profit, but we will not stand for profiteering." ; "This is possible, but only if we have ambition. Look at injectable contraceptives - 72 million women around the world accessed them in 2022. Look at COVID-19 vaccines in rich countries - 4.5 billion people were vaccinated in a year. Why can we not have the same ambition for HIV? We did it for HIV treatment and we can do it for prevention. We have done it before - and we can do it again." ; "Science has delivered a miraculous new tool: medicines that prevent HIV infection with injections just twice a year and which could work for treatment too. We must do better this time. Either companies step up, or governments step in. This is our shot to end AIDS - and we cannot afford to miss it."

a3664.speaker: One study (cited)
a3664.speech: Suggests that, if 10 million people are reached, generics could cost just $40 per person per year, a thousand times less.

a3664.speaker: The Global Fund to fight AIDS, TB and Malaria and the US President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR)
a3664.speech: Recently announced a deal to get lenacapavir to 2 million people over the next three years.

a3739.speaker: Save the Children (statement)
a3739.speech: Said on Thursday that at least four African countries will run out of specialised life-saving food for severely malnourished children in the next three months due to shortages caused by aid cuts; said supplies were getting dangerously low in Nigeria, Kenya, Somalia and South Sudan of high-energy biscuits, peanut-based Plumpy'Nut paste and other treatments known as Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF); said some clinics in the four African countries were turning to less-effective treatments for malnourished children; said stocks in Kenya are expected to run out in October and that RUTF supplies in Nigeria, Somalia and South Sudan would run out within three months; said globally, funding cuts are expected to cut off nutrition treatment this year to 15.6 million people across 18 countries, including 2.3 million severely malnourished children. Save the Children did not name specific donors or funding reductions in its statement.

a3739.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a3739.speech: Has said cuts to humanitarian aid are needed to ensure that grants align with his “America First” agenda and that other countries shoulder more of the burden.

a3739.speaker: Government officials from the four countries (Nigeria, Kenya, Somalia, South Sudan)
a3739.speech: Did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

a3739.speaker: Reuters
a3739.speech: Reported in May that cuts by the Trump administration left 60,000 to 66,000 metric tons of food, including 1,100 tons of fortified biscuits, stranded in warehouses for months earlier this year.

a3739.speaker: U.S. government
a3739.speech: Later agreed to hand over 600 tons of the biscuits to the U.N. World Food Programme but said it would have to destroy nearly 500 tons which expired last month.

a3739.speaker: U.S. State Department
a3739.speech: Announced earlier this month that it would provide $93 million for RUTF supplies to treat more than 800,000 children suffering from severe acute malnutrition in 13 countries, including Nigeria, Sudan, Kenya and Democratic Republic of Congo.

a3793.speaker: Joy Basu, U.S. Deputy Assistant Secretary of State in the Bureau of African Affairs for Economic and Regional Affairs
a3793.speech: "I am here to understand how things work economically in Benin and to find out how the United States can be a better and very good partner." ; "What explains my visit to Benin is mainly the fact that the economic connection is very important between the United States and Africa, especially as concerns the Biden administration."

a3793.speaker: Joy Basu, U.S. Deputy Assistant Secretary of State in the Bureau of African Affairs for Economic and Regional Affairs
a3793.speech: Assured: "I had the opportunity to listen to companies, members of civil society, entrepreneurs, to visit facilities such as the Autonomous Port of Cotonou and the GDIZ, and this allows us at the State Department level to see what form to give our economic cooperation to ensure that it is beneficial for both parties."

a3793.speaker: Joy Basu, U.S. Deputy Assistant Secretary of State in the Bureau of African Affairs for Economic and Regional Affairs
a3793.speech: Congratulated the Beninese government for its work in making the business environment more attractive through investments and measures such as digitalization, improved transparency and the fight against corruption; said she was impressed by the investments made towards an economy evolving very fast so as to have a positive impact on people's lives.

a3793.speaker: Joy Basu, U.S. Deputy Assistant Secretary of State in the Bureau of African Affairs for Economic and Regional Affairs
a3793.speech: Declared: "We also had the opportunity to meet the Minister of Industry and Trade and the Secretary of State for Energy. The round table with companies, civil society and other actors allowed us to learn more about the business environment in Benin, about what works and how the USA can work to strengthen economic cooperation and have a positive impact."

a3793.speaker: Joy Basu, U.S. Deputy Assistant Secretary of State in the Bureau of African Affairs for Economic and Regional Affairs
a3793.speech: "At the Autonomous Port of Cotonou, the first thing that struck me was its scale, its size, which shows how much it is a hub of trade, and it was really impressive to see the machines, the many containers that ensure the movement of goods which impact not only Benin but also its neighbours. At the GDIZ, it was really impressive to see everything that is being done in terms of processing products such as cashew nuts, cotton into textiles; it is relentless work that is very promising for Benin's economic development."
